source.title: How to spot November's planetary parade in the pre-dawn sky
source.summary: The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
source.evidence_text:
Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.
The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.
Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.
Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.
It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.
Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.
To view the parade, find a spot away from light pollution with a good view of the eastern horizon and let your eyes adjust to the dark for around twenty minutes.
The best time to view the planetary lineup is approximately 45-60 minutes before sunrise.
It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.
Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.
"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.
As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.
Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.
Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.
At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky.

grammar.concept: Relative clauses that add extra information
grammar.explanation: Use “which” to add extra information about a thing already identified, such as a planet. Put commas around this relative clause. The main sentence still makes sense if you remove the extra information.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of several objects in relation to one another, considered as a whole.
To manage to see or recognise something that is difficult to distinguish from its surroundings.
Intense light from the Sun that makes nearby objects difficult to see.
Restricted to a particular situation, place or period; here, a limited lighting condition.
Having nothing in the way that blocks the view.
Readily noticeable because something stands out strongly from its surroundings.
The capacity of a surface to send incoming light back rather than absorb it.

grammar.explanation: A pseudo-cleft uses a “what” clause followed by “be” to emphasise the information that follows. Here, the opening clause establishes what needs explaining, while the clause after “is” foregrounds the reason Venus stands out.

quiz.question: Which statement best captures the report’s central message?

November’s planetary display can be observed equally well at any point during the night.

The physical distance between them will have fallen to 1.2 degrees.

Venus sends incoming sunlight back into space, contributing to its conspicuous appearance.
Venus’s reflectivity describes how much sunlight reaches it, rather than how much it sends back.
option_feedback: “Reflectivity” concerns returning incoming light, rather than producing light independently.
The reading links Venus’s brilliance to its capacity to return sunlight.
“Reflectivity” describes the capacity to send incoming light back, not the amount of sunlight initially received.

The actual diameter of either planet.

option_feedback: The comparison gives a familiar visual reference for their 1.2-degree angular separation.
The comparison concerns the interval between the planets’ apparent positions, not their diameters.
The reading describes an angular measurement, which does not establish physical separation.

quiz.question: How should the statement that Mars, Jupiter and Regulus “may resemble a group of three stars” be interpreted?
options: The uncertainty concerns whether Regulus will be nearby, rather than whether the group will look like three stars.
It presents a possible visual impression rather than a change in what the objects are.

option_feedback: “May” qualifies the possible resemblance to three stars; the reading presents the planets’ apparent proximity to Regulus separately.
“May” qualifies the possibility, while “resemble” identifies a similarity in appearance.
The sentence offers a possible resemblance, not a guaranteed inability to distinguish the objects.

quiz.question: Which plan best follows the reading’s separate recommendations about observation and preparation?
options: Begin acclimatising 45–60 minutes before sunrise and start observing twenty minutes later.
Observe 45–60 minutes before sunrise and use that entire period as the stated minimum for eye preparation.
Observe 45–60 minutes before sunrise, allowing around twenty minutes beforehand for the eyes to acclimatise.

The reading gives around twenty minutes for eye preparation, separately from the recommended observation period.

The term concerns removing barriers to the view across the horizon.
